metadata.note: Project update, week 11. Three chapters reported separately, never summed. Ch5: 12 claims, 10 revise, 2 approved. Ch7: 32 claims, 25 revise, 5 approved, 2 pending. Ch12: 33 claims, 24 revise, 9 approved.

beats.narration: The workbooks I receive come with an automated pre-check that flags sentences for me to review. In these three chapters I learned not to trust its reasons. Several times it flagged the right sentence and pointed to a paper that did not say what it claimed.

beats.narration: I only found these by opening the papers. In Chapter 5, the pre-check said a paper found no ERBB2 changes in 224 glioblastoma patients. That paper never mentions glioblastoma. In Chapter 7, it cited a trial's design paper, written before the trial had a result. In Chapter 12, it cited a two-patient conference abstract for figures that are not in it. The flags were right. The evidence was not, so I replaced it.

beats.narration: Chapter 5 gives one statistic four times, in three different sizes: how often RAS genes are mutated in human cancer. One in four, about thirty percent twice, and about a third. I went to a 2020 study that compared every major mutation database to settle exactly this. It lands near 19 percent. The pre-check flagged three of the four. The fourth was hiding in a figure caption.

beats.new_visual_element: An approved list that was wrong three ways
beats.narration: Chapter 7 lists nine epigenetic drugs as FDA approved. Three are not. One was only approved in China and Japan. Two were withdrawn, one as recently as March 2026, which I confirmed separately because it was so recent. The list also counts one drug twice, once by name and once by its code name, and it misses three drugs that are approved.

beats.new_visual_element: A meta-analysis reported as its opposite
beats.narration: Chapter 12 reports a result backwards. It says a seven-trial analysis found a significant survival benefit, with a hazard ratio of 0.84. I read the paper. It found no significant survival benefit. The 0.84 was a different measure from the same paper, about how long the cancer took to progress.

resolver.label: THE OPPOSITE OF ITS SOURCE

beats.new_visual_element: Where to start, and where not to stop
beats.narration: In Chapter 12 I also read past the flags, through the sentences the pre-check had passed. Seven of my nineteen edits came from there, including the two worst errors in the chapter. And four of its flags did not hold up. Three fell apart once I read the book the chapter had been copied from.

beats.narration: So now I check the evidence behind a flag, not just the flag. When the same number shows up in different sizes, I treat it as a number nobody checked. And I read past the flagged rows, because that is where the worst errors were. All three chapters' corrections are now merged into the textbook.
